transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
A federal judge has blocked the Federal Communications Commission from immediately reviewing all the local TV licenses held by ABC and its corporate parent, the Walt Disney Company.
The judge ruled Wednesday the FCC "unconstitutionally" retaliated against the network for programming that angered President Trump.
Here's NPR's David folkamplick.
ABC sued after the FCC announced that it would immediately review all eight local TV broadcast licenses held by ABC and Disney.
The agency had previously launched inquiries into Disney's diversity practices and into the ABC talk show The View.
Trump had repeatedly called for ABC to be punished for its news decisions and for jabs at him by late-night comic Jimmy Kimmel.
U.S. District Court Judge Lauren Ali Khan called the threat "existential" and said the FCC's actions served to chill broadcasters' free speech.
She accused FCC Chair Brendan Carr of taking "Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders." Carr did not return NPR's request for comment.
David folkamplick, NPR News.
A Thanksgiving holiday shaping up to be a challenging one on both coasts in New Jersey, Governor Mikey Sherrill is warning residents about that storm that forced organizers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade to postpone the event until Saturday.
Sherrill says the storm could bring heavy rain, coastal flooding, and high winds.
Such high winds have the potential to down power lines, and those outages may persist as crews cannot go up in the bucket trucks and fix lines when there are sustained high winds.
In New York City, Mayor Zoram Amdani's office has issued a travel advisory for Thanksgiving Day.
On the west coast, huge waves and king tides have been battering the Bay Area, and the weather could make flying difficult.
Federal Aviation Administration reporting flight delays at Miami International Airport, where a FedEx plane overran a runway Wednesday night.
The airport says there were no injuries.
The incident happened nearly three months after an Amazon cargo jet overshot a runway in Miami, killing five people on the ground.
Trump administration has posted emails and other files on the U.S. Agency for International Development website to try to discredit the Biden administration's agenda there.
And Piers Michelle Kellerman reports.
One of the programmers that Elon Musk brought to Washington to dismantle USAID says, quote,
"You can now read internal memos showing how the agency operated.
The so-called USAID files detail the Biden administration's contacts with social media companies.
At the time, it was U.S. policy to push back on disinformation from Russia, China, and others.
But Trump administration officials say USAID was weaponized to advance a radical agenda.
The State Department says it welcomed the release of the documents and referred questions to the Office of Management and Budget, which oversees what's left of USAID.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, the State Department.
And you're listening to NPR News.
U.S. Trade Representative Jameson Greer says he does not expect increased tariffs on China, the European Union, and a dozen other trading partners to rattle the global economy.
Greer spoke to CNBC, saying the new tariffs President Trump announced Wednesday will likely not take effect for months.
Trump says this latest tariff proposal is in response to excessive factory output, leading to lower-priced products that undercut American companies.
Earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down what Trump called his "liberation day" tariffs imposed under a national emergencies law.
Seabirds treat fishing vessels like a maritime buffet, but approaching a fishing rig can snag birds and kill them,
or risks that may be underestimated according to seabirds that were employed to do some eavesdropping.
Here's NPR's Harriet Daniel.
Jonathan Rutter, a marine biologist at the University of Oxford, worked with his colleagues to attach tiny audio recorders to four shearwater seabirds off of Spain,
a Westland petrol in New Zealand, and seven northern gannets in the Celtic Sea.
Listening later, they heard this boat noise. It turned out that numerous boats showed up in the audio that didn't match public vessel tracks.
It's showing the extent of what we're not seeing.
Rutter isn't advocating for seabirds to be used as a surveillance or law enforcement tool,
but this technique reveals that the risk of seabird bycatch may be considerably higher than previously thought.
For NPR News, I'm Harriet Daniel.
And I'm Giles Snyder. This is NPR News.

topics.text: Federal judge blocks FCC from immediately reviewing ABC and Disney local TV licenses over Trump retaliation claims
New Jersey Governor Mikey Sherrill warns residents of storm that postponed Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade to Saturday
Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office issues travel advisory for Thanksgiving Day in New York City
Bay Area battered by huge waves and king tides, with flying weather disruptions expected
FAA reports flight delays at Miami International Airport after FedEx plane overran a runway
State Department releases 'USAID files' documents detailing Biden administration contacts with social media companies
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says new China and EU tariffs unlikely to rattle global economy
Oxford marine biologists use audio recorders on seabirds to reveal unseen fishing boat activity and bycatch risk
